front.title: MAP Introduction and Motivation: Autonomous Agent Interoperability

abstract.t: The Manolito Agent Protocol (MAP) is a decentralized, permissionless protocol for autonomous AI agents to discover one another by capability, negotiate work, execute it with verifiable evidence, and settle payment — without a central authority, global reputation service, or native token. This document states the problem MAP addresses, why prior designs failed, the design responses MAP adopts, and a reading guide for the rest of the specification family. The substantive specifications are the companion draft-map-*-01 documents; the critical evaluation that motivates them is 01-design-critique.md.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document family are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 [RFC2119] [RFC8174] when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here. No adaptation or weakening of these terms applies.

section.name: The Problem
section.t: Autonomous AI agents increasingly need to cooperate: one agent commissions another to run inference, call a tool, retrieve memory, or transform data. That cooperation should be verifiable, permissionless, and attriburable — any agent should be able to find a capable counterparty, agree on terms, confirm the work was done, and pay for it, without trusting a central broker with the identity graph, the reputation ledger, or the money supply.

The historical Manolito/MP2P file-sharing network (c. 2001) showed that a flat, serverless, high-churn peer network can route by what is wanted rather than where it lives. MAP evolves that instinct from "who has this file?" to "who can do this task?": the network becomes a capability graph. Several recent design sketches and a preprint (HEP v0.1) attempted exactly this, but — as 01-design-critique.md documents in detail — they contained defects that would be fatal in standards review: self-referential signature definitions, self-asserted trust scores, volatile data pushed through a global DHT, no replay protection, normative magic-weight routing, and a serialization choice that cannot support the signature semantics the documents rely on.

section.name: Why Prior Designs Failed (high level)
section.t: The critique identifies fifteen findings (C1–C15). The most consequential:

ul.li: C1 — Self-asserted trust. Advertised trust/reputation scores are

section.t: signed by the subject, proving only self-praise; a rational attacker advertises a perfect score. Any routing formula weighted by such a score is steered by attacker-controlled input.

ul.li: C2 — Non-canonical signatures. Signing Protobuf structures (which have

section.t: no canonical encoding) makes "serialize and verify" fail across implementations and enables re-serialization malleability.

ul.li: C3 — Volatile state in the DHT. Republishing load/latency every few

section.t: seconds does not scale and routes on stale fiction.

ul.li: C4 — No replay protection. Signed requests can be replayed verbatim

section.t: (re-executing paid work, double-spending receipts).

ul.li: C5 — Normative magic-weight routing. Fixed score weights freeze bad

section.t: constants into the standard and mix attacker-controlled inputs with honest ones; ranking should be local policy.

ul.li: C6 — Latency as a global field. Latency is a property of a path

section.t: between two peers, not of a node.

ul.li: C7 — Privacy leakage. Exact hardware fingerprints and broadcast query

section.t: intent link a stable identity to high-entropy metadata.

ul.li: C8 — Transport lock-in. Hard-wiring gRPC/QUIC with two parallel

section.t: identities contradicts transport-agnosticism.

ul.li: C9 — Central-bank economics. "Credits minted by the orchestrator"

section.t: reintroduces the central authority the goals forbid.

ul.li: C10 — Impractical resumption. KV-cache transfer assumes identical

section.t: engines; normative resumption must be engine-independent.

ul.li: C11 — Checkpoint trust. A checkpoint signed only by the party that may

section.t: have failed can poison its successor.

ul.li: C12 — Taxonomy anarchy. Free-text capability strings fragment the

section.t: keyspace.

ul.li: C13 — Identifier fragmentation. Three incompatible ID spaces for the

section.t: same key.

ul.li: C14 — Weakened requirements language. "RFC 2119, adapted" guts

section.t: normative force.

ul.li: C15 — Sybil hand-waving. "Reputation decay fixes Sybil" is an assertion,

section.t: not a mechanism.
The full findings, dispositions, and per-document assessment are in 01-design-critique.md.

section.name: MAP's Design Responses
section.t: Each cluster of failures maps to a concrete MAP mechanism:

tr.td: No trust fields in descriptors; trust is a local projection over dual-signed ExecutionReceipts
Deterministic CBOR (RFC 8949 §4.2.1) + COSE_Sign1; verify received bytes, never re-serialize
Two-plane discovery: stable signed descriptors in a sharded DHT; volatile status pulled on demand
msg-id + timestamp window + session sequence numbers + channel binding
Standardize verifiable inputs and hard constraints; ranking is local policy
Removed; RTT measured by the querier
Coarse hardware buckets; selective receipt disclosure; zones; relayed/decoy queries
One identity, one address book; normative bindings for libp2p/QUIC/TCP+TLS/WebSocket
Payment negotiation standardized; settlement is a pluggable registry (Lightning, stablecoins, ACH, Interledger, credit-ledger, x402)
Transcript replay (Merkle-rooted); KV-cache is an optional same-engine extension
Requester countersigns each checkpoint's transcript root
Governed capability ontology (URI) + IANA-style registry, Expert Review
One AgentID ≡ did:key ≡ libp2p Ed25519 PeerID
Proper RFC 8174 boilerplate; example domains from example.org
Layered admission costs (PoW/VDF/stake/vouch) + per-observer evidence-based trust

section.name: What MAP Is Not
section.t: To bound scope, MAP explicitly is not (see arch §4.1):

ul.li: A model-training or fine-tuning coordinator.
A general-purpose file-sharing network (content transfer exists only in

section.t: service of tasks).

ul.li: A native token, blockchain, or consensus layer.
A global, objective reputation service.
A guarantor of the semantic quality of AI outputs — MAP makes behavior

section.t: attributable and evidence-bearing, not correct.

ul.li: Wire-compatible with legacy Manolito clients (a conceptual migration guide

section.t: is in ops §7).
MAP is a protocol, not a product. "Hermes" and similar orchestrators are implementations that speak MAP; nothing in these documents privileges any implementation.

section.name: Document Map and Reading Order
section.t: The family comprises the documents listed in the README "Contents" table and the arch §11 document map. For orientation, read in this order:

ol.li: This introduction (draft-map-intro-01) — motivation and reading guide.
01-design-critique.md — the critical evaluation that justifies every

section.t: design choice (findings C1–C15).

ol.li: draft-map-arch-01 — goals/non-goals, threat model TH1–TH15, zones,

section.t: scalability, conformance classes.

ol.li: draft-map-identity-01 then draft-map-core-01 for the foundation.

section.t: governs the family.
For the complete wire format and the full code-point space in one place, consult draft-map-wire-01 (the master registry index).
Implement in the order: identity, core, discovery, tasks, then trust/pay.

section.name: Status and Maturity
section.t: Two independent, separately-authored implementations — map-rs (Rust) and map-go (Go) — reproduce every frozen test vector byte-for-byte and complete a live pairwise interop matrix (16/16 scenarios, interop/MATRIX.md) over a real transport, in both orientations. The core security properties (downgrade resistance, channel-binding session separation, delegation attenuation) are machine-checked (ops §6.3). Remaining formal work and the deferred extension semantics are listed honestly in the README "Status" section and in ops §6.3 / ops §8. The documents remain in draft pending human/expert review.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: This document is a non-normative motivational and design-rationale overview and defines no protocol mechanisms; it introduces no new security considerations. The security considerations of MAP are normative in the protocol documents — principally draft-map-core-01 (envelope, sessions, channel binding) — and the family threat model is in draft-map-arch-01.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document requests no IANA actions.
